title: Pricing by hours per project for Tiling, including floating floors
audience: Tiling and flooring contractors and supervisors who quote for wall and floor tiling and floating floors, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the business's own figures
Estimate tiling and floating-floor hours from the business's own records, including setting out, preparation, laying, curing and checking
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: Tiling is labour-heavy, and its hours are easier to see than its material costs. Setting out, subfloor preparation, cutting, laying, levelling, grouting or joining, curing time and cleaning all become hours. A floating floor adds underlay, expansion gaps, trims and transitions, which are also hours. Once the hours are known, the cost, the margin and the effect of a scope change can be seen. A flat price with no hours behind it hides risk, and it is hard to defend when a client asks why a floor costs what it does. The research for this course found no source that gives tiling or floating-floor hours per square metre, or any price per square metre, so the figures must come from the business's own job records.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in that period. Total cost includes wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, where your staff arrangements require them, vehicle running costs, adhesive, grout and sealer use, saw and tool hire, equipment, insurance, administration and premises. Productive hours are the hours a tiler spends on chargeable work, not the paid hours on a roster. Business.gov.au lists on-costs such as leave and superannuation as part of the hourly cost (Choose a pricing strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026). If a tiler is paid for 40 hours and 30 are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage. Use the business's own figures, not a figure from a general guide.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each job into tasks: each room or wall, the subfloor check, the setting-out, the laying, the trims and transitions, grouting or joining, and cleanup. Estimate each task at a standard speed for your own team, using square metres and metres from your own past jobs. Then add set-up, pack-down, travel between sites and a checking allowance. Use ranges where the job is uncertain. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as a subfloor that needs repair, late access, or a delivery delay on tiles or flooring. One guide suggests adding 10 to 20 percent to job estimates for unexpected work (Xero Australia, How to price services, 3 September 2026). That is a general service-business range, not a tiling figure, so check it against your own records. After each job, record the actual hours and the reason for any gap.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the job. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk in the job, such as an uneven or damp subfloor, a difficult layout, or a tight deadline. One author presents a gross margin of at least 20 percent as a floor, and says the right figure varies by business and market (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025). That is one author's view. Apply your materials policy and your minimum charge. If a client wants a lower price, show which room, area or extra they are asking you to remove, which keeps the discussion on the work.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A tiling quote should state the scope (areas, tile or floor type, layout approach, number of coats or underlay), the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Typical exclusions include subfloor repairs, skirting removal and refit, plumbing, waterproofing where it is outside your licence, and any structural work. Do not show the internal cost per hour unless your policy says to. Record every change to the scope and re-quote when it changes. NSW guidance says variations must be in writing and signed by both parties, and that almost all variations affect the price (NSW Consumer Building Guide, published 1 November 2025, web page modified 19 February 2026).

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten jobs of each type, such as a bathroom floor, a splashback and a floating floor. If the gap is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is not finished when it is written. It is finished when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break the job into rooms, surfaces and tasks, and estimate each task time as a range from your own records.
Add subfloor checks, set-up, pack-down, travel, curing and checking as named lines.
Multiply total crew hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin for risk and target.
Apply the materials policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only. A 35 square metre floating timber floor is to be laid in a home. The tiler's own records, which this lesson does not supply, suggest 0.5 hours per square metre for laying, plus 3 hours for the subfloor check, trims, transitions and cleanup. The tiler's cost per productive hour is taken as $60 for this example (hypothetical). No source gives either figure.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What are the crew-hours and the cost, and what must be checked before the price is issued?
workedExamples.reasoning: Laying takes 35 multiplied by 0.5, which is 17.5 hours, and the subfloor, trims and cleanup add 3 hours, so the total is 20.5 crew-hours. At the hypothetical $60 an hour the cost is $1,230. The tiler then applies a margin, as in the other lessons in this course, and checks the scope. Before the price is issued, the tiler confirms that the floor type is inside the licence rule for the state, because the NSW wall and floor tiling page does not mention floating floors. The hours and the rate in this example are arithmetic for the method only and are not benchmarks.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet or spreadsheet with room-by-room and square-metre hours
Time log for each job, with estimated and actual columns
Measuring tape or laser measure for area and layout
Moisture meter and level or straightedge where the site provides one

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, adhesives and grout, tools, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out subfloor checks, curing time and set-up
commonErrors.prevention: Name them as separate lines on every quote.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a floating floor with no exclusions or subfloor condition
commonErrors.prevention: List the subfloor condition assumed, the exclusions, and what the client must provide.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each job and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026). State and territory fair trading rules also apply, and they differ between states.

Tiling work can need a licence or registration, and the scope and value can decide it. In NSW, a contractor licence is needed for wall and floor tiling valued over $5,000 in labour and materials including GST. In Victoria, floor and wall tiling is a limited class of domestic building work, and floating floors are not addressed in the source read. The Victorian sources read word the $10,000 threshold three ways ('more than $10,000', '$10,000 or more' and 'over $10,000'), and the single-trade treatment of tiling-only work is not settled, so treat the threshold as unresolved and check it against the Victorian Act and with the Victorian Building Authority before use. In Queensland, wall and floor tiling is a licensed class and does not mention floating floors. Check each state's rule before quoting a floating floor. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the business's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten jobs of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision, a minimum-charge check and a licence check for the type of work and its value.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Tiling quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours, by square metre where relevant
summary: Hours make tiling work visible, so start every quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Subfloor checks, curing and travel time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid tiler, and nothing else from the accounts
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and any bonus
The average hourly rate of competitors and any figure from a general guide
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, adhesives and tools, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A floor is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a floating-floor quote need an exclusions list and a stated subfloor assumption?
options: To hide the margin from the client and keep the rates secret from the crew
To show what the price covers, so subfloor work and scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To make the quote longer and fill the page with more text
To lower the client's expectations and make the job seem smaller than it is

business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as leave and superannuation belong in the hourly cost.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; a 10 to 20 per cent buffer for unexpected work (general service range, not a tiling figure).

New Zealand publisher. Supports: comparing quoted and actual labour to correct the next quote. The 20 per cent gross margin floor is one author's view.

Markel Direct, 'How to price a job as a tradesperson', https://www.markeluk.com/knowledge-centre/how-to-price-a-job-as-a-tradesperson, dated 12 August 2026. Supports: listing every task, including site visits, travel, set-up and cleanup, before estimating hours.

Supports: the licence threshold of over $5,000 in labour and materials including GST; floating floors not mentioned.

States 'more than $10,000'. Threshold unresolved.
